title: [Chapitre] IX et IX bis. [Ateliers] : notes manuscrites (05-15/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is a methodological aside ('Remarques, sur l'introduction des I_{<a}, I_{>b}. Autre présentation') inside a 1986 series of combinatorial notes. The previous page stated a theorem about cos-Ψ°, s-Ψ°, Omb° (shadows), the complementary presheaf Φ* and flags Drap(L). The next page treats interior, redundant, lacunary and isolated vertices of a 'préfaisceau' L and their exchange under L ↦ L*.

The page restarts from the simplest model.

1. A 'combinatorial oriented segment', which Grothendieck suggests might better be called a 'pseudo-segment', is a system (I, ∂I) with ∂I = {ω0, ω1}. Here I is a finite ordered set (in context, a linearly ordered set of subdivision points) with least element ω0 (origin) and greatest element ω1 (extremity), and ω0 < ω1, i.e. card I ≥ 2. The interior is I° = I \ ∂I.

2. The degenerate case card I = 2, i.e. I° = ∅, is the 'indivisible segment'. It gives exactly one simplicial multiplicity, the oriented standard 1-simplex Δ^1.

3. For a non-degenerate I one would also use the half-open pieces I_{<a}, I_{>b}. In the indivisible case these auxiliary structures are not needed. The theory of the complementary presheaf L* of a presheaf L on I can then be built using only vertices I_a (a ∈ I) and closed intervals I_{a,b} (a < b).

In modern terms: a 'presheaf' L is a subcomplex of the 1-dimensional cell complex given by subdividing a segment at the points of I. L* is its complementary (dual) subcomplex, a one-dimensional combinatorial Alexander/Lefschetz-type duality. The I_{<a}, I_{>b} handle the boundary behaviour at the ends ω0, ω1. The page explains why those extra pieces appear in the theorem on the previous page (hypotheses on whether L_{≤a}, L_{≥b} belong to Φ) and why they can be dropped in the simplest case.
errors: No mathematical error. Minor looseness: 'ensemble ordonné fini' is not explicitly said to be totally ordered, though the segment interpretation and the notation I_{a,b} with a<b suggest a chain.
The equivalence ω0 < ω1 ⇔ card I ≥ 2 is correct once a least and a greatest element are assumed.

ideas.what: Combinatorial oriented segment: a finite (linearly) ordered set with distinct least and greatest elements, with boundary ∂I={ω0,ω1} and interior I\∂I
ideas.modern_name: Finite strict interval / bipointed finite linear order (objects of Joyal's interval category, dual to Δ)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Joyal (Disks, duality and Θ-categories, 1997) for the interval–Δ duality; the notion itself is classical
ideas.where_published: Pursuing Stacks discusses 'segments' and intervals in test categories, but not in this exact combinatorial form

ideas.what: The indivisible segment (card I = 2) corresponds to the simplicial multiplicity Δ^1
Complementary presheaf L* of a sub-presheaf of a subdivided segment, describable using only vertices I_a and intervals I_{a,b}

missed.claim: The 'segment orienté combinatoire' (finite ordered set with distinct min ω0 and max ω1) is precisely the notion of a finite strict interval later used by Joyal for the duality Δ^op ≃ intervals. In context, Grothendieck combines it with a complementation operation L ↦ L*, a duality-on-intervals viewpoint that predates Joyal's paper. The link is only implicit on this page.
missed.quote: "segment orienté combinatoire" ... d'un ensemble ordonné fini doté d'un plus petit élément ω0 ou origine, et d'un plus grand élément ω1 ou extrémité
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is of minor historical interest as an independent 1986 appearance of the interval category and of complement-duality on subdivided segments. The page itself gives no new result.

deep.surprise_reason: This is an expository restart of an elementary combinatorial setup: an ordered segment, its boundary, the indivisible case Δ^1, and complements. It is well known in substance. The only faint interest is the implicit anticipation of the interval/Δ duality viewpoint.
transcription_corrections: The page number at the top is '13' (it sits between pages 12 and 14), not '17'.
First line 'C. pullback' is doubtful; the image shows a short abbreviated heading ('C. p...l...t.'), probably not 'pullback'.

Main text 'qui donne lieu à une singularité qui est une multiplicité simpliciale' more likely reads 'qui donne lieu à une multiplicité qui est une multiplicité simpliciale' (a struck word replaced by 'multiplicité').
The left-margin note likely reads something like 'C'est le seul cas où on a une multiplicité simpliciale' rather than '...une singularité'; it is uncertain.
The insertion under (I,∂I) reads roughly '(com[me] ... d'un segment orienté)', i.e. a gloss on the pair (I,∂I) as an oriented segment.
